subject: binary
title: Why Everything Runs on Two Symbols
summary: Binary trades compactness for reliability; bit width fixes range in advance; and meaning lives in the encoding, not the bits.

keys.prompt: Why do nearly all computers use binary, even though it takes more digits than decimal?
keys.answer: Two well-separated states are simple to build with logic gates and resist noise. Extra digits are cheap; misreads are not.

keys.prompt: How does an integer's bit width set its range?
keys.answer: n bits encode 2^n values, 0 to 2^n − 1 if unsigned. Each extra bit doubles the range, and the width is fixed in advance.

keys.prompt: Why did Unicode keep ASCII's first 128 codes unchanged?
keys.answer: Compatibility: a UTF-8 file of plain ASCII characters is byte-for-byte identical to an ASCII file, so old text and software kept working.

cards.title: The verbose winner
cards.text: Write 37 in decimal and it takes two digits. In binary it takes six: 100101. For people, base 2 is clumsy. Yet almost every modern computer uses it. The reason is physics and engineering, not elegance.

cards.question: An unsigned 32-bit integer starts at 0. About how large a number can it hold, in billions?
cards.reveal: 2³² − 1 = 4,294,967,295, about 4.3 billion. Thirty-two on/off switches cover a range that big.

cards.title: Physics picks base 2
cards.text: Binary wins because two states are easy to build and hard to confuse. Logic gates implement it directly. With only two well-separated voltage levels, moderate noise doesn't change the reading. Early machines used switches, punched holes and paper tape; disks use magnetic polarity. Any physical system with two distinct states can hold a bit.
cards.example: The trade is length for reliability: 37 needs six bits instead of two decimal digits, but each bit is far harder to misread.

why.q: Why is noise immunity worth more than compact notation?
why.a: Adding digits is cheap. A misread value silently corrupts data. Two far-apart states trade length for reliability.

cards.title: Width is decided up front
cards.text: An n-bit unsigned integer encodes 2ⁿ values, from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. The growth is exponential: 8 bits reach 255, 32 bits reach 4,294,967,295. But a stored integer has a fixed width chosen in advance. Too few bits and the range runs out; too many and every value costs extra memory.
cards.example: Each added bit doubles the range. Going from 32 to 33 bits adds another 4,294,967,296 possible values.

examples_by_interest.business: Say an order system numbers invoices with an unsigned 16-bit integer. It tops out at 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535, so a growing business would outrun it. A 32-bit field pushes the ceiling past 4.29 billion.

cards.title: Meaning lives in the encoding
cards.text: Bits carry no meaning of their own. The pattern 1101001 is 105 as an unsigned integer and lowercase i in ASCII. Integers can also be stored as binary-coded decimal or Gray code. Every file format and protocol is an agreement about how to read patterns, and a mismatched agreement turns valid data into nonsense.
cards.example: 105 = 64 + 32 + 8 + 1, so the same seven bits serve as a number or a letter depending only on the rule applied.

why.q: Why can't software just inspect bits and infer what they mean?
why.a: The same pattern is valid under many encodings at once. Only the agreed rule, usually set by the format or protocol, says which was meant.

cards.title: Standards lock in
cards.text: ASCII, first published in 1963, mapped 128 characters to 7-bit codes, and its punctuation shaped programming-language syntax. It was English-focused, with no accented letters. Unicode kept ASCII as its first 128 code points, so a UTF-8 file of plain ASCII is identical to an ASCII file. UTF-8 overtook older encodings on the web in 2008.
cards.example: Compatibility made switching cheap: old ASCII text needed no conversion at all.

why.q: Why did UTF-8 extend ASCII instead of starting clean?
why.a: Keeping the first 128 codes identical meant existing ASCII text was already valid UTF-8, so old files and software kept working.

cards.title: From theology to switches
cards.text: Leibniz wrote his first known work on binary in 1679 and published his best-known article on it in 1703; he saw 1 and 0 as a symbol of creation out of nothing. In 1937, Claude Shannon's MIT master's thesis implemented Boolean algebra and binary arithmetic with relays and switches, essentially founding practical digital circuit design.
cards.example: The math was ready for centuries. What made it dominant was a physical device whose two states mapped onto it cleanly.

cards.question: ASCII's English-first design was a sensible trade-off in 1963 that carried real costs later. Where in your own work is a 'good enough' standard or field width quietly locking in today's assumptions?
nudges: Think of IDs, account numbers, form fields or file formats you depend on.
Argue the other side: when is fixing a standard early worth its later costs?

questions.q: A counter is stored as an unsigned 16-bit integer. What is the largest value it can hold?

options.why: Right: 2¹⁶ − 1. Sixteen bits give 65,536 values, starting at 0.
That's how many values there are. Counting from 0, the top is one less.
Range grows exponentially with width, not by a fixed amount per bit.
That's the five-digit decimal maximum. Binary places double rather than multiply by 10.

questions.q: What's the main reason computers are built on binary rather than decimal hardware?

options.text: Two well-separated states are simple to build with logic gates and resist noise
options.why: Yes. Reliability and simple circuits outweigh the longer numbers.

options.text: Binary numbers are shorter than decimal ones
options.why: They're longer: 37 is two decimal digits but six bits.

options.text: Leibniz's 1703 paper set it as a standard
options.why: Leibniz described the math; circuits made it practical much later.

options.text: Decimal values can't be stored in circuits at all
options.why: They can, for example as binary-coded decimal. Binary is a design choice.

questions.q: Why did Unicode keep ASCII's first 128 code points unchanged?

options.text: So existing ASCII text and software stayed valid
options.why: Exactly. Plain ASCII files are already valid UTF-8.

options.text: Because no encoding can hold more than 128 characters
options.why: Unicode holds far more. It kept the 128 for compatibility.

options.text: Because ASCII already covered every language
options.why: ASCII was English-focused. Unicode exists to cover much more.

options.text: To make each character exactly one bit shorter
options.why: The goal was compatibility, not saving bits.

sources.title: Binary number
sources.supports: Binary is base 2 and uses only 0 and 1; each digit is a bit; almost all modern computers use it because it is straightforward to implement with logic gates and has noise immunity; in a modern computer bits may be two different voltages, on disks magnetic polarities, earlier switches and punched holes or tape; any mechanism with two exclusive states can represent bits; counting goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100 with reset and carry like decimal; each bit is an increasing power of 2 and the value is the sum, e.g. 100101 = 32 + 4 + 1 = 37; Leibniz's first known binary work was 1679 and his best-known article, Explication de l'Arithmetique Binaire, was published in 1703; he saw 1 and 0 as a symbol of creation out of nothing; Claude Shannon's 1937 MIT master's thesis implemented Boolean algebra and binary arithmetic with relays and switches and essentially founded practical digital circuit design.

sources.title: Integer (computer science)
sources.supports: Integers are commonly stored as a group of bits; an integral type with n bits can encode 2^n numbers, and an unsigned type typically represents 0 through 2^n - 1; other encodings such as binary-coded decimal, Gray code or printed character codes are sometimes used.

sources.title: ASCII
sources.supports: ASCII encodes 128 code points (0 to 127), storable in 7 bits; lowercase i is 105; first edition published in 1963; lowercase letters differ from uppercase by a single bit, which simplified case-insensitive matching and building keyboards and printers; its punctuation shaped programming-language syntax; it lacks accented letters (e.g. resume with accents); the first 128 Unicode code points are the same as ASCII, making UTF-8 backward compatible with 7-bit ASCII; UTF-8 overtook older encodings as the most common on the web in 2008.
